usable_content: This study performed untargeted metabolomics on plasma samples from a large cohort of renal cell carcinoma (RCC) patients treated with nivolumab (anti-PD1) in the CheckMate 025 trial. The authors identified that higher baseline plasma levels of the purine metabolite inosine were significantly associated with longer overall survival (mOS 33 months vs. 22 months for low levels) specifically in the ICB-treated group, but not in patients treated with everolimus. This provides quantitative clinical evidence linking a specific microbial-derived metabolite to ICI response outcomes. The study is a narrative review summarizing the biochemical properties, sources, and biological functions of inosine in gut homeostasis and colorectal cancer (CRC). It identifies specific bacterial taxa (e.g., *Bifidobacterium pseudolongum*, *Lactobacillus* spp.) as producers of inosine. Mechanistically, it describes how microbial-derived inosine enhances immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) efficacy by activating T cells via adenosine A2A receptors, increasing IFN-γ production, and promoting M1 macrophage polarization in preclinical mouse models (MC38, CT26). It also notes that CRC cells can use inosine as an alternative carbon source under glucose restriction. The study reports on one phase-2 clinical trial where oral inosine was added to PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor therapy in a mixed solid-tumor population, showing mild enhancement of efficacy and reduced toxicity, but explicitly states that CRC-specific results were not reported separately. The study reports clinical cohort data linking fecal Short-Chain Fatty Acid (SCFA) concentrations to Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor (ICI) outcomes. Specifically, in a cohort of 52 solid tumor patients receiving anti-PD-1 therapy (nivolumab or pembrolizumab), higher fecal concentrations of acetate, propionate, butyrate, and valerate were significantly associated with longer progression-free survival [29]. Additionally, in a smaller cohort of 11 non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients receiving second-line nivolumab, gut microbial metabolites including propionate and butyrate were significantly associated with long-term beneficial effects [34]. Conversely, the study also cites evidence that high serum butyrate and propionate concentrations were negatively correlated with ICI efficacy in patients treated with anti-CTLA-4 (ipilimumab) [35]. Regarding Inosine, the study describes its role primarily through preclinical mouse models (bladder and small bowel cancer), noting it improves anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-L1 efficacy by regulating Th1 differentiation via the A2aR-cAMP-CREB axis, but does not provide human physiological concentration data for Inosine in TME or serum linked to response.
